_meta.comment: Original KaiSip CIA Part 3 practice questions for Section C (Quality of the Internal Audit Function), written from KaiSip's own notes and the opened Global Internal Audit Standards (2024). No IIA practice question, textbook or prep-bank text used. Not affiliated with or endorsed by The IIA. Pilot cia3_d3_001 to cia3_d3_010, 25 Nov 2026.

domain_name: Quality of the Internal Audit Function

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Quality assurance and improvement program. A risk manager runs the self-assessment
questions.question: Dalia, chief audit executive of a Lebanese bank's three-person function, asks the risk manager, a former internal auditor who knows the Standards well, to run the periodic self-assessment. Which view of this is MOST accurate?

options.A: Acceptable, and it also meets the external assessment requirement
options.B: Not acceptable: self-assessment is for internal audit staff
options.C: Acceptable as an internal assessment, not as an external one
options.D: Acceptable, provided an outside assessor validates the results

questions.key_concept: Periodic self-assessments may be done by people elsewhere in the organization who know internal audit practice; they never count as independent external assessments.
questions.pre_read: Recall who Standard 12.1 allows to perform internal assessments, and whom Standard 8.4 treats as independent.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 12.1 lets internal assessments be performed by the function itself or by others in the organization who know internal audit practice well enough, so a risk manager who was an internal auditor qualifies. Standard 8.4's considerations treat anyone from another department as not independent, so the work cannot stand in for the external assessment. Option D borrows independent validation, which belongs to the external route, not to internal assessment.

wrong_explanations.A: Someone from another department sits outside internal audit but inside the organization, so the work cannot count as an independent external assessment.
wrong_explanations.B: Standard 12.1 lets people elsewhere in the organization who know internal audit practice well enough perform internal assessments.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: independent validation is how a self-assessment can meet the external requirement; an internal assessment needs no outside validation to be acceptable.

tips: Eliminate: A, because another department is never independent enough for an external assessment, and B, because Standard 12.1 allows knowledgeable people from elsewhere in the organization.
Final two: C beats D because independent validation belongs to the external route; an internal assessment by a knowledgeable insider needs none.
Exam cue: on CIA quality questions, sort the assessor first: inside the organization means internal assessment, whatever the department.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Quality assurance and improvement program. An assessor whose designation lapsed
questions.question: Hiroshi, a Japanese rail operator's chief audit executive, proposes an independent firm's external assessment team: a lead whose Certified Internal Auditor designation has lapsed, an accountant and an IT specialist. Which change is MOST needed?

options.A: Include someone whose Certified Internal Auditor designation is active
options.B: Add a member with experience as a chief audit executive
options.C: Replace the accountant and the IT specialist with active designation holders
options.D: Swap the IT specialist for an auditor from the parent company

questions.key_concept: The external assessment team needs at least one member holding an active Certified Internal Auditor designation; other qualifications are considerations.
questions.pre_read: Recall what Standard 8.4 requires of the assessment team's qualifications, and what it only suggests weighing.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 8.4 requires the chief audit executive, in choosing the assessor or team, to make sure one or more of its people hold an active Certified Internal Auditor designation. A lapsed designation does not count, so the team falls short until someone with an active one is on it. Experience as a chief audit executive is among the qualifications the considerations suggest, useful but not required, so option B ranks below the requirement.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: senior internal audit leadership is a qualification the considerations suggest weighing; the requirement still unmet is an active Certified Internal Auditor.
wrong_explanations.C: One active Certified Internal Auditor on the team is the requirement; swapping out the accountant and IT specialist would also lose skills the review needs.
wrong_explanations.D: An auditor from a parent company comes from a related organization and is not considered independent for an external assessment.

tips: Eliminate: C, because one active designation holder meets the requirement and other skills add value, and D, because people from a parent company are not independent for this purpose.
Final two: A beats B because an active Certified Internal Auditor is a requirement, while chief audit executive experience is a suggested qualification.
Exam cue: on CIA external assessment questions, check the one firm qualification first: at least one active Certified Internal Auditor.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Quality assurance and improvement program. Reporting a self-assessment's results
questions.question: A periodic self-assessment at a Chilean copper miner finds two nonconformances with the Standards. What is MOST clearly required in chief audit executive Ignacio's report to the board and senior management?

options.A: The results, once both nonconformances have been put right
options.B: The results, with an independent assessor's validation of them
options.C: The results, with senior management's approval of the fixes
options.D: The results, with action plans and their proposed timelines

questions.key_concept: Periodic self-assessment results go to the board and senior management with action plans and a proposed timeline for the nonconformances found.
questions.pre_read: Recall what Standard 12.1 requires the chief audit executive to do with the results of periodic self-assessments.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 12.1 requires the chief audit executive to build action plans, with a proposed timeline, for the nonconformances and improvement chances a periodic self-assessment finds, and to communicate the results and the plans to the board and senior management. Waiting until both are fixed, option A, delays what the board needs to oversee quality and skips the plan it is meant to agree. Validation and senior management approval are not part of this step.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: fixing the gaps is the aim, but the results and dated action plans go to the board and senior management now, not after the repairs.
wrong_explanations.B: Independent validation is a route to meeting the external assessment requirement; internal assessment results are reported without it.
wrong_explanations.C: Senior management gives input, but the report needs action plans with a timeline, and the considerations have actions agreed with the board.

tips: Eliminate: B, because independent validation belongs to the external assessment route, and C, because the report needs dated action plans, and actions are agreed with the board.
Final two: D beats A because results and dated action plans are reported now, so the board can oversee the fixes rather than hear of them afterward.
Exam cue: on CIA quality questions, a self-assessment's results travel with action plans and a timeline to the board and senior management.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Quality assurance and improvement program. Topical Requirements in quality assessments
questions.question: Planning a Greek port authority's periodic self-assessment, chief audit executive Eleni hears an audit manager say Topical Requirements are topic rules outside the quality program. Which reply is MOST accurate?

options.A: Agreed: assessors judge conformance with the Standards, not topic rules
options.B: Not so: quality assessments evaluate conformance with them as well
options.C: Partly: the external assessment checks them, internal ones do not
options.D: Not so: the board checks conformance with them each year

questions.key_concept: Topical Requirements are mandatory for assurance work, and conformance with them is evaluated in quality assessments, internal and external.
questions.pre_read: Recall what a Topical Requirement says about documenting applicability and about quality assessments.
questions.correct_explanation: Each Topical Requirement makes conformance mandatory and says quality assessments will evaluate it, and it requires kept evidence that every requirement was assessed for applicability, with reasons for any exclusion. Standard 8.3's program covers every aspect of the function through internal and external assessments, so Eleni's self-assessment checks Topical Requirement conformance too. Option C limits that to the external assessment, which neither source does.

wrong_explanations.A: Topical Requirements are mandatory and used with the Standards; the requirement itself says quality assessments evaluate conformance with it.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the external assessor does check them, but the quality program covers every aspect of the function, internal assessments included.
wrong_explanations.D: The board considers quality results when it assesses the function, an essential condition; conformance itself is evaluated in the quality assessments, internal and external.

tips: Eliminate: A, because conformance with a Topical Requirement is mandatory for assurance work and assessed, and D, because the board oversees results rather than assessing conformance.
Final two: B beats C because quality assessments, internal ones included, evaluate Topical Requirement conformance; the program covers every aspect of the function.
Exam cue: on CIA quality questions, Topical Requirements sit inside the quality program; keep applicability records for the assessors.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Disclosing nonconformance with the Standards. What the record must contain
questions.question: A Hungarian airport's board defers its external assessment past the five-year limit until an internal audit merger ends; chief audit executive Bence records the circumstance and reason. What else MOST needs recording?

options.A: The alternative actions taken and the impact of those actions
options.B: A firm target date for completing the deferred external assessment
options.C: A statement that the rest of the function conforms
options.D: A statement from the planned assessor on current conformance

questions.key_concept: A nonconformance record states four things: the circumstance, the alternative actions taken, their impact and the rationale.
questions.pre_read: Recall the four elements Standard 4.1 requires the chief audit executive to document and communicate when a requirement cannot be met.
questions.correct_explanation: When a requirement cannot be met, Standard 4.1 requires the chief audit executive to document and communicate the circumstance, the alternative actions taken, the impact of those actions and the rationale. Bence has two of the four. A target date, option B, is sensible and fits the action plans Standard 12.1 asks for after self-assessments, but it is not one of the elements this disclosure must carry.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a date helps the board track the fix, and self-assessment action plans carry timelines, but Standard 4.1's elements are circumstance, alternative actions, impact and rationale.
wrong_explanations.C: Conformance elsewhere is expected, but a statement of it is not one of the four elements; the record still lacks the alternative actions and their impact.
wrong_explanations.D: No assessor has reviewed the function yet; a nonconformance record is the chief audit executive's own account, not an assessor's statement.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a statement about the rest of the function is not one of the four elements, and D, because the record is the chief audit executive's account, made before any assessor arrives.
Final two: A beats B because alternative actions and their impact are required elements, while a target date belongs to other action plans.
Exam cue: on CIA nonconformance questions, check for all four elements: circumstance, alternative actions, impact and rationale.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Disclosing nonconformance with the Standards. A law that blocks one requirement
questions.question: A state secrecy law bars a Vietnamese shipyard's internal auditors from keeping the engagement documentation the Standards require for naval contracts. Which approach by chief audit executive Thao is BEST?

options.A: Cite the secrecy law as a requirement used with the Standards
options.B: Disclose the function's nonconformance with the Standards as a whole
options.C: Conform with all other parts and disclose the part the law blocks
options.D: Leave the matter for the external assessor to judge and report

questions.key_concept: When a law prevents conformance with part of the Standards, the function conforms with every other part and discloses the part it cannot meet.
questions.pre_read: Recall what Standard 4.1 requires when laws or regulations prohibit conformance with part of the Standards.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 4.1 requires that, when a law or regulation prohibits conformance with any part of the Standards, the function conform with all the other parts and make appropriate disclosures, with the chief audit executive documenting the circumstance, alternative actions, impact and rationale. Option A applies a different rule in 4.1: citing other authoritative requirements used alongside the Standards. A secrecy law that blocks a requirement is a nonconformance, not an added framework.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Standard 4.1 does require citing other authoritative requirements used with the Standards, but a law blocking a requirement is a nonconformance that must be disclosed.
wrong_explanations.B: Only the blocked part is a nonconformance; Standard 4.1 requires conformance with every other part, so a blanket statement overstates the gap.
wrong_explanations.D: Disclosure is the chief audit executive's duty now; the external assessor later uses that record and never replaces it.

tips: Eliminate: B, because only the blocked part fails and the rest still binds, and D, because the chief audit executive discloses now rather than leaving it to an assessor.
Final two: C beats A because a law that stops conformance creates a nonconformance to disclose, while citing other requirements is for frameworks used alongside the Standards.
Exam cue: on CIA questions where a law blocks one requirement, conform with the rest and disclose the blocked part.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Disclosing nonconformance with the Standards. A gap that reaches the whole function
questions.question: A self-assessment at a Zambian bank finds its internal audit plan has rested for two years on an undocumented risk assessment. Which step is MOST clearly required of chief audit executive Mwila?

options.A: Disclose it in the final communication of each later engagement
options.B: Disclose it and its impact to the board and senior management
options.C: Tell senior management, which decides whether the board hears it
options.D: Document this year's assessment and treat the gap as closed

questions.key_concept: A nonconformance affecting the whole function goes, with its impact, to the board and senior management; a one-engagement gap goes in its own final communication.
questions.pre_read: Recall where Standards 12.1 and 15.1 send a nonconformance, depending on whether it affects one engagement or the whole function.
questions.correct_explanation: Standards 12.1 and 8.3 require the chief audit executive to report internal assessment results, with action plans, to the board and senior management, and 12.1 adds that a nonconformance affecting the function's overall scope or operation goes to both with its impact. A plan without the documented risk assessment Standard 9.4 requires shapes every engagement, so it reaches the function as a whole. Option A is Standard 15.1's route for one engagement's nonconformance.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Standard 15.1 puts one engagement's nonconformance in its final communication; this gap sits in the plan behind every engagement, so both bodies hear it.
wrong_explanations.C: A function-wide nonconformance must go to both the board and senior management; senior management cannot filter what the board receives.
wrong_explanations.D: Documenting this year's assessment fixes the cause, but two years of plans rested on undocumented assessments; that nonconformance is still reported with its impact.

tips: Eliminate: C, because senior management cannot decide what the board hears about nonconformance, and D, because fixing the cause does not remove the duty to disclose.
Final two: B beats A because a gap in the plan reaches the whole function, so it goes to the board and senior management, not into engagement reports.
Exam cue: on CIA nonconformance questions, match the route to the reach: one engagement in its report, the whole function to the board and senior management.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Performance measures for internal audit. A scorecard with no targets
questions.question: Chief audit executive Sophie's scorecard for a Belgian insurer reports plan completion, key-risk coverage and board satisfaction, each beside last year's figure; an analyst validates the figures' accuracy quarterly. What does it MOST lack?

options.A: A findings count per auditor to show productivity
options.B: A periodic check that the reported figures are accurate
options.C: Countable measures in place of board satisfaction
options.D: A target for each measure, set against its objective

questions.key_concept: Each performance objective needs targets, quantitative and qualitative; a measure with no target shows a trend but not success or shortfall.
questions.pre_read: Recall what Standard 12.2's considerations say about targets, qualitative measures and checking the accuracy of reported measures.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 12.2's considerations say the chief audit executive should set quantitative and qualitative targets to track progress toward each performance objective, and should periodically validate the accuracy of reported measures. Sophie's figures are checked quarterly, so accuracy is covered; what is missing is any level to judge them against. Beside last year's figure, a measure shows direction, not whether the objective is met.

wrong_explanations.A: Judging auditors by the number of findings can impair objectivity, as Standard 2.2's considerations warn; it adds volume, not a target.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: validating accuracy is a step the considerations suggest, but the stem says an analyst already validates the figures every quarter.
wrong_explanations.C: The considerations call for qualitative as well as quantitative targets; board satisfaction shows value that counts alone miss.

tips: Eliminate: A, because findings counts can harm objectivity, and C, because qualitative measures such as board satisfaction belong in a balanced set.
Final two: D beats B because the figures' accuracy is already validated each quarter; without targets they still cannot show whether objectives are met.
Exam cue: on CIA scorecard questions, every measure needs a target; a trend alone shows direction, not achievement.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Performance measures for internal audit. A falling action plan completion rate
questions.question: A Thai hotel group's rate of action plans completed with the intended result fell from 80 to 55 percent; a director calls it internal audit's failure. Which reply by chief audit executive Niran is BEST?

options.A: Disagree: the rate measures management alone, not internal audit
options.B: Agreed: the rate measures how well internal audit follows up
options.C: Partly: it reflects management's follow-through as well as internal audit's
options.D: Partly: a shared result, and internal audit should help finish the actions

questions.key_concept: Action plan completion is a useful measure, but management completes actions, so the rate is not internal audit's performance alone.
questions.pre_read: Recall what Standard 12.2's considerations say about measuring the share of action plans that achieve the desired outcome.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 12.2's considerations list the share of action plans management completes with the desired outcome as a measure internal audit may track, and note it is not only a reflection of internal audit's performance: management is responsible for completing the actions and achieving the outcomes. Niran should read the drop as a shared signal worth analyzing, not as the function's failure. Option B treats a shared measure as internal audit's alone.

wrong_explanations.A: Management completes the actions, but the considerations call the rate not exclusively internal audit's performance, so it still says something about internal audit's work.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: internal audit tracks the rate and follows up, but management completes the actions, so the rate is not internal audit's performance alone.
wrong_explanations.D: Internal audit confirms that actions are implemented; completing them stays with management, and taking them on would leave internal audit assessing its own work.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the considerations treat the rate as partly internal audit's, and D, because internal audit confirms actions and leaves completing them to management.
Final two: C beats B because management completes the actions and internal audit tracks them, so the rate reflects both, not internal audit alone.
Exam cue: on CIA performance questions, ask who controls the result a measure counts before calling it internal audit's performance.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Performance measures for internal audit. Savings beside a quality shortfall
questions.question: A Peruvian port's internal audit function finished its plan 15% under budgeted hours, but quality reviews found a third of workpapers did not support conclusions. Which reading by chief audit executive Lucía is BEST?

options.A: Efficient, but the workpaper gap is an issue needing an action plan
options.B: Efficient; report the savings and fix the workpapers internally
options.C: Next year's budget can drop to the hours actually used
options.D: Workpaper reviews are supervision tools, not performance measures

questions.key_concept: Read performance measures together: an efficiency gain does not show good performance when quality falls, and a shortfall needs an action plan.
questions.pre_read: Recall what Standard 12.2 requires once measures reveal an issue, and what Standards 8.3 and 12.1 count when judging quality.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 12.2 requires the chief audit executive to develop an action plan for issues the performance measures reveal, and Standard 8.3 requires internal assessment results, ongoing monitoring included, to reach the board and senior management. Finishing under budget looks efficient, but workpapers that do not support conclusions undercut the results the board relies on. Option B fixes the workpapers out of view, reporting only the favorable measure.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the savings are real, but fixing quality quietly hides it from the board and senior management, who receive quality results and the action plans that address them.
wrong_explanations.C: Cutting the budget to the hours used would lock in the conditions behind the weak workpapers before their cause is known.
wrong_explanations.D: Standard 12.1's considerations name supervisory reviews of workpapers as a primary way to monitor conformance and performance, so their results are performance evidence.

tips: Eliminate: C, because cutting hours before finding the quality gap's cause could deepen it, and D, because quality reviews are part of monitoring the function's performance.
Final two: A beats B because a quality shortfall the measures reveal needs an action plan, and quality results reach the board rather than being fixed out of view.
Exam cue: on CIA measures questions, set speed or cost results beside quality results before calling the function's performance good.
